nameStory: The pink lady's slipper gets its charming name from its distinctive flower, which looks remarkably like a delicate Victorian lady's ballet slipper or moccasin. The pouch-shaped petal forms a perfect little shoe, complete with a slit opening that insects must squeeze through. Some folks call it the moccasin flower, honoring its resemblance to soft Indigenous footwear.
description: The pink lady's slipper is one of New England's most enchanting wild orchids, featuring a single dramatic pink flower that dangles between two large, pleated leaves. This woodland gem grows 6-15 inches tall and produces just one flower per plant, making each discovery feel like finding hidden treasure. The inflated pink pouch serves as an elaborate trap for pollinating bees, while the two broad basal leaves spread horizontally from the base like welcoming arms.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single pink pouch-shaped flower with a deep slit down the front, flanked by twisted reddish-brown petals that look like ribbons - the pouch feels papery and slightly inflated when gently touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two large oval leaves at the base with prominent parallel veins running lengthwise - they feel thick and slightly fuzzy with deep pleated ridges you can trace with your finger

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single flower stem rises between the two basal leaves with no leaves on the flowering stalk itself - the whole plant has a distinctive candelabra-like silhouette

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Brown capsule develops after flowering, splitting open to release thousands of dust-like seeds that feel almost weightless when blown from your palm

habitat: Pink lady's slippers thrive in acidic, well-drained soil under mature coniferous or mixed forests, often among pine, hemlock, and oak trees. Look for them on slight slopes or raised areas where the soil stays moist but not soggy, frequently growing alongside blueberries, wintergreen, and various ferns. They prefer dappled sunlight filtering through the forest canopy rather than deep shade or full sun.

seasonality.spring: Flowers bloom from late May through June, with the pink pouches at their most vibrant. The two distinctive pleated leaves emerge in early May and are easily spotted even before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: After flowering ends in July, the leaves remain green and photosynthesizing while the seed capsule develops and matures. Plants are still identifiable by their characteristic two-leaf pattern.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-brown and begin to wither by September. The dried seed capsule may persist, splitting open to release seeds on windy autumn days.
seasonality.winter: All above-ground parts disappear completely, leaving only the underground root system dormant until spring. No winter identification features remain visible.

funFact: Pink lady's slippers are elaborate con artists that trick bees into pollinating them without offering any reward - bees fall through the slit into the pouch, get trapped, and must crawl out through a specific exit route that forces them to pick up pollen, but they get absolutely no nectar for their trouble!
confusionNotes: Before flowering, pink lady's slippers could be mistaken for young trout lily, but trout lily has mottled leaves while lady's slipper leaves have solid green color with parallel veins. Remember: "Trout are spotted, slippers are not" - trout lily leaves have distinctive brown mottling that lady's slippers completely lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "lady's slipper," this plant takes 10-17 years to mature enough to produce its first flower, and it may skip flowering entirely in stressful years. Many people don't realize that picking the flower often kills the entire plant since it disrupts the delicate relationship with soil fungi that the orchid depends on for survival.
compareHints: Pink lady's slipper is the only lady's slipper orchid in New England with just two basal leaves and a pink pouch. Yellow lady's slipper has multiple leaves arranged up the stem and a bright yellow pouch, while showy lady's slipper has white petals with a pink-striped pouch and grows much taller in wetter areas. The rare ram's-head lady's slipper has a distinctly conical white pouch with red veining that looks nothing like the inflated pink balloon of this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the pink lady's slipper which has two basal leaves and a solid pink pouch, the showy lady's slipper has multiple stem leaves and a white pouch with pink markings.
Yellow lady's slipper is the only bright yellow slipper orchid in New England.
Ram's-head is much smaller than its lady's slipper relatives and has unique twisted petals that spiral backward like ribbons.
